The VR intervention targeted contrast sensitivity and contour integration, and perceptual organization was assessed using the Jittered Orientation Visual Integration (JOVI) task. Primary analyses focused on participants who completed the task at baseline, mid-treatment, and post-treatment (N = 50; VR: n = 26; AC: n = 24). Linear mixed-effects models examined JOVI performance as a function of treatment condition, timepoint, and task difficulty (jitter), with planned contrasts testing differential change over time. A significant treatment condition × timepoint interaction indicated that changes in performance differed between groups. Planned difference-in-differences contrasts showed that the VR group exhibited greater improvement from baseline to mid-treatment (estimate = 5.03, p < .001) and from baseline to post-treatment (estimate = 4.30, p = .005) relative to AC. VR targeting low- and mid-level visual processes improved perceptual organization performance relative to an AC condition in participants with a schizophrenia spectrum disorder. These effects emerged early in training and persisted to the post-treatment assessment, supporting the effectiveness of interventions targeting visual processes for improving perceptual organization in this population.

title: Unpacking associations between trauma types and schizotypy dimensions in a community sample.
abstract: Interpersonal trauma (IT; intentionally harming another individual), is an established risk factor for psychosis-spectrum symptoms. However, few studies have investigated whether differential risk based on trauma type (IT versus non-IT) extends across major dimensions within schizotypy. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether increased risk associated with IT reflects the nature of the trauma or a 'dose' effect from accumulation of trauma, as IT occurs more often. Aiming to inform risk assessments, we employed a large community sample (N = 506) to address these gaps. A schizotypy measure distinguished cognitive perceptual (CP), disorganized (DO), constricted affect/affiliation (CA), and excessive social anxiety (SA) factors. Using participant report of IT and non-IT, an analysis of variance approach examined schizotypy associations with each trauma type and their co-occurrence. We then tested how adding cumulative trauma impacted results. We hypothesized IT would be associated with schizotypy factors relevant to social threat (SA; CP which includes paranoia), even after controlling for cumulative trauma. While IT was robustly associated with elevations on all schizotypy factors, above and beyond the effect of non-IT, cumulative trauma still added significant explanatory power particularly for CP and to a lesser extent DO. Interestingly, for SA, only IT showed significant associations, even when cumulative trauma was added. Results remained when controlling for demographics, general psychopathology, and cannabis use. Our findings underscore the importance of both trauma type and trauma dose when assessing risk for schizotypy. Future work should investigate mechanisms by which exposures may contribute to differential symptom expression.

title: Coupling of action-intention binding is reduced in aphantasia.
abstract: The sense of agency (the feeling of being the cause of one's own actions) is thought to arise from reliability-weighted integration of multiple cues across the intention-action-outcome sequence. Whether integration is coordinated across the stages of this sequence or carried out independently at each stage remains unknown. Using the Libet clock intentional binding task in 578 participants spanning the aphantasia-to-hyperphantasia spectrum, we examined the correlation between action binding and intention binding as an index of this coordination. At the group level, negative coupling between individuals' action and intention binding was present in typical imagers (r = -0.27, p < .001), but was not present in core aphantasia, where voluntary visual imagery is entirely absent (r = -0.05, p = .44). Coupling differed significantly between these two groups, even though neither binding component differed between them. Individuals with weak but present imagery (hypophantasia) showed a distinct binding profile, with intention binding exceeding action binding magnitude, a pattern absent in all other groups. Together these findings suggest that it is the coordination of integration across the action sequence, rather than the strength of individual binding components, that distinguishes those with and without voluntary imagery.

title: Forgotten lobotomies in Rome: new evidence of psychosurgery in postwar Italy.
journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
abstract: The history of psychosurgery, perhaps the most controversial venture in clinical neuroscience's past, has long been written without Rome. While leucotomies and lobotomies performed have been documented in northern and southern Italian centres, the Italian capital - despite being the birthplace of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and home to two major state psychiatric institutions - has remained largely absent from historical accounts. Drawing on previously unexamined archival materials from Italy and the United States, and despite substantial gaps in the surviving documentation-including the inaccessibility of all but one patient record-, this study reconstructs psychosurgical activity in Rome between 1949 and the early 1950s, identifying interventions performed both at the University Neuropsychiatric Clinic and at the Santa Maria della Pietà Asylum. The Roman experience reveals an ambivalent attitude toward psychosurgery. Although new surgical modifications were proposed locally, growing scientific and ethical concerns soon emerged, leading, at least in one of the two institutions, if not both, to the eventual abandonment of the initiative. By restoring Rome to the history of psychosurgery, this study challenges established narratives of postwar Italian clinical neuroscience and highlights the early emergence of doubts surrounding lobotomy.

title: PM2.5 exposure and retinal neurovascular dysfunction: Clinical and mechanistic evidence for complement C3/C3aR pathway involvement.
abstract: PM2.5 is a pervasive environmental toxicant associated with retinal neurodegeneration, yet the mechanisms remain unclear. This study combined clinical, animal, and cellular approaches to investigate whether C3/C3aR signaling mediates PM2.5‑induced retinal neurovascular damage. In retrospective longitudinal glaucoma cohort, a linear mixed‑effects model analyzed PM2.5 effects on inflammatory markers. In mice, we examined PM2.5 effects on retinal complement, microglia activation, neurovascular function, and vision. The protective effect of the C3aR blocker SB290157 was also evaluated. BV2 and retinal endothelial cells were used to study C3‑dependent microglial polarization and its vasoregulatory effects. In clinical experiment, we identified a significant association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and systemic complement dysregulation, characterized by a decrease in serum C3c. In mice, PM2.5 exposure induced marked retinal C3 activation. This change was characterized by microglial activation, vascular dysfunction, and retinal structural and functional impairment. In vitro, PM2.5 directly induced C3/C3aR-dependent microglial M1 polarization and stimulated endothelial vasoconstrictor secretion via microglial crosstalk. Treatment with C3aR inhibitor attenuated the vicious cycle, preserving retinal structure and visual function. In conclusion, C3/C3aR axis serves as a key mechanistic link between PM2.5 exposure and retinal neurodegeneration. Targeting this pathway may offer a therapeutic strategy for mitigating pollution-related retinal damage.

title: Experience in action: Using art-science activities to explore experiences of movement and the body in Parkinson's and autism.
abstract: To explore possible new directions for sensorimotor research, we created experiential workshops for people with lived experience. Seven people with Parkinson's and six older autistic adults attended artist-led drop-in art-science workshops, designed with advisors with lived experience. Open-ended activities based on sensorimotor experiments provoked spontaneous and unexpected conversations between visitors and researchers about their experiences of movement and the body. We invite others to apply this informal playful approach, which was both enjoyable and effective in generating future research ideas.

title: Transition From Child to Adult Care in Paediatric Neurological Disorders in Europe-A Joint EAN-EPNS Survey of Current Practices for Healthcare Providers.
abstract: Transition from paediatric to adult care is essential for young people with paediatric-onset neurological disorders, yet remains inconsistently structured across Europe. This study aimed to characterise current transition practices, identify key barriers and explore perceived priorities for improving transition care. A cross-sectional web-based survey, developed by the European Paediatric Neurology Society/European Academy of Neurology Task Force on Transition from Childhood to Adulthood, was distributed to members of both societies between February and April 2025. The 22-item questionnaire assessed institutional characteristics, transition practices, perceived barriers and improvement measures. Responses were analysed descriptively and compared according to the reported presence of an institutional transition programme. Overall, 328 responses were analysed. A transition programme was reported to be available in the country of practice by 123 respondents (37.5%). Respondents from institutions with transition programmes reported earlier transition initiation (median 16 vs. 17 years) and more frequent structured practices, including joint paediatric-adult consultations (73.7% vs. 27.1%). The highest-rated barriers were lack of multidisciplinary teams, limited adult neurology capacity and difficulty accessing adult neurology services. Key improvement priorities included joint consultations, national recommendations, specialised care networks and dedicated transition coordination. Satisfaction with current transition practice was low; only 7.9% of respondents reported complete satisfaction. Transition of care for paediatric-onset neurological disorders in Europe remains heterogeneous. Although core elements of effective transition are widely recognised, implementation is limited by organisational and system-level barriers. Coordinated strategies are needed to support structured, patient-centred transition pathways.

title: The FOG-COA Protocol: Validation of Freezing of Gait Clinical Outcomes Assessments in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: The development and evaluation of novel treatment options for freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease have been limited by an ambiguous definition and lack of standardized clinical outcome assessments (COAs) that 1) reliably assess FOG severity, 2) are responsive to change, and 3) capture patient-relevant impact. To address these gaps, working groups from the International Consortium on FOG (ICFOG) developed a clinician-rated outcome-the Giladi Protocol for assessing FOG severity (GP-FOG), and a patient-reported outcome-the FOG Quality of Life questionnaire (FOG-QOL). The FOG-COA project will evaluate the conceptual framework and psychometric properties of these COAs to determine their fit-for-purpose in clinical trials. A total of 105 freezers and 35 non-freezers from seven international centers will complete the GP-FOG in the dopaminergic OFF and ON states during two separate visits (7-14 days apart). FOG annotations from video recordings will be used to assess criterion validity. OFF and ON GP-FOG scores from two trained raters at Visit 1, as well as within-rater scores across visits, will examine reliability. Responsiveness will be evaluated by comparing effect sizes between OFF and ON GP-FOG scores. Patient meaningfulness will be assessed through the association between patient-perceived FOG severity and GP-FOG scores. Participants will complete the FOG-QOL at each visit to assess test-retest reliability and validity against the NFOGQ and PDQ-8. A subset of freezers will undergo cognitive interviews to identify relevant daily life FOG impacts and evaluate FOG-QOL meaningfulness. Collectively, this work will advance standardized, sensitive, and meaningful FOG-COAs, supporting regulatory-grade endpoints and the development of a multi-dimensional outcome framework.

title: Remote Video Assessment of Ataxia via SARAhome: Correlation of Pose-Derived Endpoints with Clinician Severity Ratings.
abstract: Remote assessment of ataxia is increasingly important for patient-centered care and clinical research. SARAhome, a validated video-based adaptation of the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA), enables self-administration of key motor tasks at home. The aim was to evaluate the correlation of pose-derived gait and stance endpoints from SARAhome videos with clinician-rated severity. In a multisite observational study, participants recorded SARAhome tasks on consumer mobile devices via the Atom5TM app. Clinicians rated videos using standardized criteria, blinded to automated outputs. Kinematic measures were extracted via pose estimation and aggregated to video-level features. Videos were aggregated per participant before correlation using Spearman's ρ and Kendall's τ, with 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. We analyzed 5418 gait and stance videos from 58 participants across 4 sites (gait n = 2205, stance n = 3213). Score distribution was skewed toward lower severity. For gait, clearance variability (ρ = 0.52 [0.37-0.64]) and median-normalized base of support (ρ = 0.51 [0.35-0.66]) correlated most strongly with item ratings, followed by shoulder sway root mean square (ρ = 0.43 [0.24-0.60]). Adjusted foot clearance (worse limb) correlated negatively (ρ = -0.35 [-0.52 to -0.15]). For stance, anteroposterior sway (ρ = 0.51 [0.36-0.65]), leg alignment variability (ρ = 0.51 [0.36-0.65]), and composite sway (ρ = 0.48 [0.32-0.62]) were most associated with severity. Base of support widened monotonically with severity and was the most reliable gait feature (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.88). Pose-derived digital endpoints from home-captured SARAhome videos show robust, clinically interpretable correlation with severity, supporting scalable remote phenotyping. Findings motivate longitudinal validation toward clinical and regulatory utility.

title: TGF-β Inhibition Attenuates Tau Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Patient-Derived Organoids.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a devastating 4-repeat tauopathy with no approved disease-modifying treatments. Recent evidence showed increased transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) levels in PSP patient-derived ventral midbrain organoids (vMOs) and serum neuronally derived exosomes. This study investigated whether TGF-β pharmacological inhibition could mitigate PSP pathology in vMOs. Ninety-six vMOs were generated from induced pluripotent stem cells from two PSP-Richardson's syndrome patients and two healthy control donors (HCs). From day 60 to day 90, PSP organoids were (1) exposed to TGF-β receptor I inhibitor (SB431542); (2) exposed to recombinant TGF-β1, TGF-β2, and TGF-β3; or (3) untreated. At day 90, several tau species were assessed by immunoblotting; neurodegeneration was evaluated through TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], neurofilament light chain [NfL]); astrocytic activation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) marker was evaluated by immunofluorescence, and histopathological hallmarks were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. An HC-derived organoid subgroup was exposed to the treatment conditions to assess potential toxicity. At day 90, untreated PSP-derived vMOs exhibited increased phosphorylated tau levels (Ser396, Thr181, Ser202/Ser205 [AT8]) compared with HC-derived vMOs, dopaminergic neuron loss (reduced TH, increased NfL), and astrocytic reactivity (increased GFAP), along with PSP characteristic tau deposition. Tau hyperphosphorylation, neurodegeneration, and astrocytic reactivity were all markedly reduced in PSP-derived vMOs treated with TGF-β receptor I inhibitor. Conversely, exposure to TGF-β exacerbated these features. No toxic effects were observed in HC vMOs exposed to treatment conditions. Pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling prevented key PSP molecular alterations in patient-derived organoids. These findings support further research and pave the way for future investigation of TGF-β-targeting strategies in clinical trials in patients with PSP. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and α-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: Accumulating evidence indicates that habitual diet, including plant-based dietary patterns, is associated with neurodegenerative α-synucleinopathy risk. However, the role of diet and its correlation with the gut microbiome in prodromal α-synucleinopathy, specifically among patients with isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), remains unclear. To evaluate dietary patterns, their interplay with gut microbial dysbiosis, and longitudinal effects on neurodegenerative progression in iRBD patients. We recruited 287 iRBD patients and 208 age- and sex-matched controls. Plant-based diet indices (PDIs) were derived from food frequency questionnaires. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed in 456 subjects for diet-microbiome analyses. After a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 45 (15.7%) iRBD patients converted to α-synucleinopathies. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the associations between diet and neurodegenerative outcomes. We found that iRBD patients exhibited lower healthful PDIs (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.48 [0.29-0.80], P = 0.005) but higher consumption of unhealthful plant-based foods (refined grains, sweets, and sweeteners). Diet-microbiome interaction analysis identified dietary associations for 84.3% of iRBD-related gut microbes, including co-occurrence between healthful PDI and Clostridium sp. AF20-17LB. Longitudinally, four dietary factors and five iRBD-related microbes were associated with neurodegenerative outcomes; specifically, higher coffee consumption was linked to a lower risk of progression to α-synucleinopathy (aHR [95% CI]: 0.30 [0.11-0.78], P = 0.01). Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that the iRBD-enriched species Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans mediated the association between unhealthful PDI and dementia-first conversion. Habitual diet in iRBD is associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis and predicts neurodegenerative progression. These findings highlight diet-microbiome interactions as modifiable targets for intervention in prodromal α-synucleinopathy. © 2026 The Author(s). Movement Disorders published by Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

title: Effects of postmortem interval on myelin integrity in rhesus macaque brain tissue.
abstract: When conducting microscopy of human brain sections, the postmortem interval (PMI) introduces myelin-related artifacts that can confound neuropathological interpretation, yet the extent and detectability of these changes remain poorly characterized. This study examined the impact of controlled PMI on myelin integrity in rhesus macaque brain tissue using advanced optical imaging approaches. Brains from five aged rhesus macaques (20.5-28.5 years) were maintained at 4°C and analyzed at 0, 24, and 72 h postmortem. Myelin integrity in white and gray matter was assessed using quantitative birefringence microscopy to measure relative retardance and polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to quantify scattering coefficients, retardance, and volumetric features. Increasing PMI was associated with progressive myelin degradation, reflected by significant reductions in relative optical retardance in white matter (p < 0.01) and gray matter (p < 0.001), alongside increased scattering coefficients in both regions (p < 0.001). Morphological analyses revealed a marked increase in myelin defects per mm2 with longer PMI (p < 0.001), characterized by swellings, vesicles, and structural discontinuities. These findings demonstrate that PMI causes significant detectable myelin changes, which can be quantified using optical imaging techniques, providing critical implications for interpreting postmortem neuropathological studies (especially with human brain tissues) and establishing a need for standardized PMI considerations in research protocols to ensure accurate pathological assessment in neurological disease investigations.

title: Early Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in Type 1 Fucosidosis: Reversal of Central Tegmental Tract Abnormalities.
abstract: Fucosidosis is an ultra-rare lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency, leading to progressive neurodegeneration and multisystem involvement. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has emerged as a potential disease-modifying therapy, particularly when performed early in the disease course. However, neuroradiological reversibility after HSCT remains insufficiently documented. We report a male infant diagnosed with Type 1 fucosidosis at 6 months of age based on enzymatic and genetic analyses. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) demonstrated characteristic abnormalities, including central tegmental tract involvement. The patient underwent allogeneic HSCT at 14 months of age and was followed clinically and radiologically. Following HSCT, the patient demonstrated stabilization and gradual improvement of neurological functions. Follow-up neuroimaging revealed marked regression of white matter abnormalities and reversal of central tegmental tract hyperintensities. Developmental progression improved after transplantation, and no major transplant-related neurological complications occurred. Early HSCT was accompanied by clinical improvement and resolution of central tegmental tract abnormalities in this patient. These imaging changes may help assess treatment response, though larger cohorts and longer follow-up are needed to evaluate long-term outcomes.

title: Beyond Excitotoxicity: Glutamate-Independent Mechanisms Underlie Noise-Induced Synaptopathy and Compromise Gene Therapy for Hereditary Deafness.
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is classically attributed to glutamate excitotoxicity, yet the precise requirement for synaptic glutamate release remains untested using genetic approaches. Here, we investigated noise-induced cochlear damage using Vglut3 knockout (Vglut3-KO) mice, which lack glutamatergic transmission from inner hair cells. Following 116 dB SPL noise exposure, wild-type (WT) mice exhibited permanent threshold shifts, persistent ABR wave I amplitude reduction, and significant loss of both ribbon synapses and outer hair cells (OHC) in the basal turn. Unexpectedly, Vglut3-KO mice also exhibited significant synapse loss despite their inability to release glutamate, revealing glutamate-independent mechanisms of synaptopathy. Proteomic analysis of noise-exposed cochleae identified 62 differentially expressed proteins enriched in synaptic and extracellular matrix pathways, including upregulation of Rps6ka1, Cplx2, and Cdk5, and downregulation of Ppa2. Comparative profiling of Vglut3-KO mice further revealed 233 differentially expressed proteins, with widespread downregulation of synaptic, mitochondrial, and ECM pathways. Importantly, noise exposure severely compromised AAV8-Vglut3 gene therapy efficacy in Vglut3-KO mice: while unexposed mutants achieved complete functional recovery, noise-exposed animals failed to attain normal hearing thresholds, with VGLUT3 expression restored across all cochlear turns as confirmed by immunofluorescence. These findings demonstrate that high-intensity noise induces synaptopathy through both excitotoxic and non-excitotoxic mechanisms involving synaptic and ECM disruption, and that acoustic trauma creates persistent OHC loss limiting gene therapy outcomes, underscoring the need for comprehensive otoprotective strategies in hereditary deafness patients awaiting treatment.

title: Local-Global Spherical Sliced Wasserstein Graph Kernel for Schizophrenia Identification.
abstract: Accurate identification of schizophrenia (SZ) using functional connectivity (FC) is fundamentally challenged by the non-Euclidean geometry of neuroimaging data and information loss from arbitrary graph thresholding. To overcome these bottlenecks, this study proposes the local-global spherical sliced Wasserstein graph (LG-SSWG) kernel. By embedding FC profiles onto a hyperspherical manifold, the proposed framework utilizes geodesic optimal transport to construct a mathematically rigorous, positive-definite graph kernel. This threshold-free approach synergistically integrates macroscopic whole-brain topology and region-specific functional architectures. Evaluated on the public COBRE dataset, LG-SSWG achieves a superior 84% accuracy, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Beyond predictive accuracy, the method exhibits strong clinical interpretability by identifying critical neuroanatomical biomarkers, particularly the left thalamus and right precuneus. Network analysis reveals pervasive functional hyperconnectivity within subcortical relays and cognitive networks in SZ patients. Notably, this hyperconnectivity correlates positively with PANSS positive symptom scores. Consequently, these altered thalamocortical and precuneus-anchored circuits indicate that SZ clinical symptoms may be closely associated with disrupted sensory gating and functional segregation. Ultimately, the LG-SSWG kernel provides a principled geometric learning tool that advances both the objective diagnosis and mechanistic understanding of schizophrenia.

title: VPS13A Disease (Chorea-Acanthocytosis) in Puerto Rico; New Genetic and Clinical Observations.
abstract: VPS13A disease is a very rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in the VPS13A gene. Its prevalence appears to be relatively high in Puerto Ricans, although limited genetic information has been available. To describe the genetics of VPS13A disease (chorea-acanthocytosis) in Puerto Rico. Data were obtained from Puerto Rican patients with genetically confirmed VPS13A disease. Eighteen cases were identified, all carrying at least one of four mutations, c.1400_1401del, c.3556_3557dup, c.3889C>T, and c.2825-253_2905-374del (exon_27-deletion); six additional single variants were detected. Seizures were the presenting symptom in 53% of patients. The presence of these probable founder mutations could explain the apparently increased prevalence in Puerto Rico; half of the described variants are newly described mutations and half have been previously reported. Enhanced clinical awareness of the spectrum of presenting symptoms and diagnostic clues, and improved access to genetic testing are essential for timely diagnosis in this population.

title: Reduced finite-dimensional model of two-dimensional protein cluster formation.
abstract: The aggregation or clustering of proteins plays an important role in the formation of postsynaptic domains (PSDs) at excitatory and inhibitory synapses in neurons. PSDs are rich in scaffolding proteins that can transiently trap transmembrane neurotransmitter receptors, allowing them to regulate the strength of synaptic connections during learning and memory. Recently, a two-dimensional diffusion-mediated aggregation model of PSD formation was developed in which the spatial locations of the clusters are determined by a set of fixed anchoring sites. The system is kept out of equilibrium by the recycling of particles between the cell membrane and interior. This results in a nontrivial stationary state consisting of multiple stable protein clusters. In this paper, we use matched asymptotic methods to reduce the underlying reaction-diffusion model with moving interior boundaries to a corresponding finite-dimensional nonlinear system. The latter couples the cluster radii to the spatially averaged protein concentration in the bulk domain. We assume that the diffusivity D is O(1/ν), where ν=-1/lnε and ε is a small parameter that characterizes the size of the clusters relative to the size of the bulk domain. The reduced dynamical system allows us to explore both the existence and stability of the multicluster stationary state while maintaining the effects of diffusion-mediated interactions between clusters.

title: Kinetic energy in random recurrent neural networks.
abstract: High-dimensional chaotic dynamics can emerge in a large random recurrent neural network when the synaptic gain crosses a threshold. Recent works showed that the kinetic energy of neural activity links the chaotic dynamics and the supporting unstable fixed points (equilibria) in the phase space. Here, we investigate the kinetic-energy-centric properties of random recurrent neural networks by combining dynamical mean-field theory with extensive numerical simulations. We find that the average kinetic energy shifts continuously from zero to a positive value at the known critical value of coupling variance (synaptic gain) and exhibits a cubic scaling behavior near the critical point from above. This scaling behavior is supported by numerical simulations and provides a quantitative characterization of how fast the dynamics change during the onset of chaos as well as how far the chaotic dynamics are away from the unstable fixed points. The steady-state activity distribution is further calculated by the theory and compared with simulations on finite-size systems from the kinetic-energy optimization perspective as well. The activity distribution is also analyzed in a geometric angle, revealing that although the original chaotic dynamics and the gradient dynamics of the kinetic energy are arranged in a shell-like structure, they are well separated in the polar direction. The trajectory length on the chaotic manifold can be derived from the stationary kinetic energy, and the associated stationary behavior is analyzed as well.

title: Information retention by synaptic learning rules in stochastic spiking neural networks.
abstract: Physical learning systems require a means to store information about the past. In the brain, information is thought to be stored in synaptic connections between neurons whose weights change in response to pre- and postsynaptic action potentials, or spikes, according to specific plasticity rules. To date, most models of synaptic plasticity are derived from in vitro studies in which spike times are under precise experimental control, but whether these models generalize to in vivo regimes of high spike time variability is not known. To shed light on this problem theoretically, here I estimate the mutual information between Poisson spike trains in a network of neurons and the synaptic weight updates they trigger via different plasticity rules. Although most synaptic plasticity models propose correlation- or coincidence-based rules based on the measurement of pre- and postsynaptic spike times, I show that such rules do not always maximize information storage. In the biologically important, energy-efficient operating regime of low firing rates and sparse plasticity, rules that simply count pre- and/or postsynaptic spikes in fact store more information per synapse than spike-timing-dependent rules that measure coincidence events. In such regimes, spikes are more common than coincidences hence better able to transmit information into synaptic weights. It may in turn be advantageous to encode information to be stored as spike counts, or time averages, rather than correlations. The theory suggests a normative account for recently discovered noncanonical hippocampal plasticity rules in vivo and predicts that spike-timing-dependent rules will be preferentially active in neural circuits operating at higher firing rates.

title: Limits of optimal decoding under synaptic coarse-tuning.
abstract: Sensory information propagates through successive processing stages in the brain, where synaptic weight patterns between stations determine how downstream neurons decode information from upstream populations. Although optimized synaptic connectivity can enhance information transmission, it requires precise weight tuning. Recent evidence depicting substantial synaptic volatility raises two fundamental questions: How does coarse-tuning of synaptic connectivity affect information transmission? What strategies could the nervous system employ to maintain reliable communication despite synaptic fluctuations? We addressed these questions by analyzing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for binary stimulus discrimination under two decoding schemes: a naive population average and an optimized linear decoder. For the naive decoder, we found that SNR remains largely insensitive to synaptic imprecision, since performance is already limited by correlated noise in neuronal responses. For the optimal decoder, we identified three distinct regimes, that is, weak, moderate, and strong coarse-tuning. Under weak coarse-tuning, SNR squared scales linearly with population size N. Under moderate coarse-tuning, scaling becomes sublinear. Strikingly, under strong coarse-tuning, the regime most consistent with observed neuronal heterogeneity, SNR saturates and cannot be improved by recruiting larger populations. This limitation persists even when incorporating feedforward or recurrent network architectures. These findings suggest that in the biologically relevant regime of strong coarse-tuning, naive and optimal decoders can achieve qualitatively similar performance. The analysis shows that effective readout under synaptic volatility is constrained to an invariant low-dimensional manifold aligned with the naive decoder, potentially pointing to a fundamental principle for robust neural computation in the face of ongoing synaptic remodeling.

title: Evolutionary chemical learning in dimerization networks.
abstract: We present a framework for chemical learning based on competitive dimerization networks (CDNs)-systems in which multiple molecular species, e.g., proteins or DNA-RNA oligomers, reversibly bind to form dimers. We show numerically that these networks can, in principle, be trained in vitro through directed evolution, enabling the implementation of complex learning tasks such as multiclass classification without digital hardware or prior knowledge of all microscopic association constants. Each molecular species functions analogously to a neuron, with binding affinities acting as tunable synaptic weights. A training protocol involving mutation, selection, and amplification of DNA-based components allows CDNs to robustly discriminate among noisy input patterns. The resulting classifiers exhibit strong output contrast and high mutual information between input and output, especially when guided by a contrast-enhancing loss function. Comparative analysis with in silico gradient descent training reveals closely correlated performance. These results establish CDNs as a promising platform for analog physical computation, bridging synthetic biology and machine learning, and advancing the development of adaptive, energy-efficient molecular computing systems.

title: Numerical investigation of the impact of neural stem cells on brain tumors.
abstract: Malignant brain tumors, including glioblastoma and medulloblastoma, remain highly treatment-resistant. Neural stem cells (NSCs) are being investigated as tumor-tropic therapeutic vectors, but the temporal interaction between tumor and NSC populations requires quantitative characterization before model-based treatment hypotheses can be interpreted reliably. This study aimed to develop and numerically evaluate a reproducible 2-population model of tumor-NSC dynamics and to quantify the influence of NSC persistence and NSC-mediated tumor killing on simulated tumor burden. A normalized system of 2 coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations was used: dT/dt = rT(1 - T) - βTN and dN/dt = αN(1 - N) - γTN. The baseline simulation used r = 0.20000 day-1, α = 0.05000 day-1, β = 0.35000 day-1, γ = 0.30000 day-1, T0 = 0.50000, and N0 = 0.40000. Explicit Euler integration was performed with Δt = 0.01 day over 20 days. A descriptive nonlinear regression fit, Fourier spectral analysis, 1-parameter sensitivity analyses, and joint α-β sensitivity analysis were applied to the simulated trajectory. In the baseline simulation, tumor density decreased from 0.5000 to a minimum of 0.4772 at day 2.59 (4.57% below the initial value) and subsequently increased to T20 = 0.8273, while NSC density declined from 0.4000 to N20 = 0.0247. The descriptive regression reproduced the simulated tumor trajectory with R2 = 0.9973 and root mean square error = 0.00590. Increasing α from 0.05 to 0.10 day-1 reduced T20 by 12.6% relative to baseline, and increasing β from 0.35 to 0.50 day-1 reduced T20 by 19.9%. Jointly setting α = 0.10 and β = 0.50 day-1 yielded T20 = 0.4427, 46.5% below the baseline terminal tumor density. The Fourier spectrum was dominated by the zero and low-frequency components, with no distinct oscillatory peak over the 20-day window. The model indicates that NSC persistence and NSC-mediated tumor killing materially influence terminal tumor burden, but the baseline parameterization produces only transient early suppression followed by tumor regrowth as the NSC population declines. The results are population-level, model-based estimates rather than tumor-type-specific clinical efficacy measures. Tumour-specific calibration, spatial migration, immune interactions, and experimental validation are required before translational conclusions can be drawn.

title: Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy: A comprehensive review of pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management.
abstract: Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (CCM) is a prevalent yet frequently underrecognized cardiac complication of liver cirrhosis, characterized by impaired myocardial contractile reserve, diastolic dysfunction, and electrophysiological abnormalities. Despite its clinical significance, particularly in the setting of liver transplantation, CCM remains largely overlooked. We performed a narrative review of the literature on CCM published up to December 2025, covering pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, imaging modalities, biomarkers, and management strategies. Depending on the diagnostic criteria used, the prevalence of CCM ranges from 29% to 67.2%. Advanced imaging techniques, particularly global longitudinal strain and cardiac magnetic resonance, enable early detection of subclinical systolic dysfunction. A "toxic triangle" comprising systemic inflammation, metabolic derangements, and neurohormonal activation represents an integrated pathophysiological model that drives myocardial fibrosis and dysfunction. Beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists remain mainstays of pharmacological management, while liver transplantation is currently the only definitive therapy. CCM is an underrecognized condition with substantial clinical implications. Standardized diagnostic criteria, validated biomarkers, and large-scale prospective studies are urgently needed to improve patient outcomes.

title: Research engagement and visibility in a specialized pediatric rehabilitation profession: A bibliometric review of Italian neuro and psychomotor therapists of developmental age, 1993-2025.
abstract: In Italy, the neuro and psychomotor therapist of developmental age (Terapista della Neuro e Psicomotricità dell'Età Evolutiva [TNPEE]) is a specialized healthcare rehabilitation professional focusing on neurological and developmental disorders in children from birth through age 18. As this profession exists exclusively in Italy and has no direct international counterpart, its scientific contribution is difficult to identify using conventional bibliographic searches. This bibliometric analysis aimed to map the identifiable TNPEE-authored scientific literature, describe publication patterns and thematic areas, and examine research output according to institutional and academic affiliation. Major scientific databases and complementary author-, institution-, network-, and citation-based search strategies were used to identify publications involving verified TNPEEs through March 8, 2025. Bibliometric indicators described publication volume and temporal trends, authorship patterns, institutional affiliations, academic appointments, and primary research areas. Temporal trend analyses were restricted to complete calendar years 1993 to 2024. The analysis identified 138 distinct TNPEE authors contributing to 507 publications published between 1993 and March 8, 2025. Temporal analyses of the 497 publications from complete calendar years 1993 to 2024 showed a marked increase in output over time. Research themes predominantly encompassed neurodevelopmental disorders, cerebral palsy, neuromuscular conditions, and early intervention strategies. Publication output was concentrated among the 6 TNPEEs holding university appointments, who contributed to 218 (43%) of identified publications. This study maps the visible scientific contribution of TNPEEs and highlights challenges in professional identification and bibliographic retrievability. Bibliometric data alone cannot establish the determinants of the observed concentration of research output; dedicated workforce, qualitative, and institutional studies are needed. Standardized professional identification may improve the bibliographic traceability of research contributions from nationally defined healthcare professions.

title: Examining Social Comparison in Relation to Disordered Eating and Depressive Symptoms in Older Women.
journal: The International journal of eating disorders
abstract: The main aim of this study was to examine social comparison as a transdiagnostic factor for disordered eating and depression in older women. Ninety-six women ages 65 and older completed a survey online or on paper that included the assessment of general comparison, body-specific comparison, restrictive eating, bulimic symptoms, depressive symptoms, and self-compassion. Both general comparison and body-specific comparison were positively associated with restrictive eating, bulimic symptoms, and depressive symptoms (rs: 0.26-0.48). Self-compassion attenuated the association between general comparison and bulimic symptoms, as well as the associations between body-specific comparison and both restrictive eating and depressive symptoms. The combination of high levels of comparison and low levels of self-compassion was associated with the highest levels of psychopathology. Social comparison and self-compassion appear to have transdiagnostic roles, as potential risk factors and protective factors, respectively, for older women across disordered eating and depression. Given elevations in disordered eating and depression in older women, considering social comparison and self-compassion as part of a transdiagnostic approach is worth exploring.

title: Enhancing Antifungal Activity of Nitric Oxide-Releasing Polymers via the Incorporation of Piperine.
journal: Journal of biomedical materials research. Part B, Applied biomaterials
abstract: As hospital-acquired infections and antibiotic and antifungal resistance increase, there is a need for constant innovation of novel antimicrobial solutions. To this end, the endogenous free-radical gas nitric oxide has been explored, as nitric oxide kills bacteria effectively at low levels without producing significant cytotoxic effects. Biomaterials can be designed to release nitric oxide by incorporating nitric oxide donor molecules such as S-nitrosothiols. Though nitric-oxide-releasing materials show excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial activity, their efficacy against fungal species is limited. This work aims to combine nitric oxide release via an S-nitrosothiol, S-nitroso-N-acetylpenicillamine, with the release of a natural antifungal compound, piperine, from a commercially available biomedical polymer, CarboSil. In this work, a polymer platform was successfully developed that does not induce cytotoxicity while causing statistically significant reductions in the adhered and planktonic microbial loads of two bacterial strains and one fungal strain. This material is promising for preventing hospital-acquired and biomaterial-associated infections in short-term applications.

title: ProSAAS overexpression arrests progression of motor deficits in a rat alpha-synuclein model of Parkinson's disease.
Neighborhood stress and social vulnerability in relation to placental metals concentrations.
abstract: Recognizing that social and environmental exposures may co-occur and impact perinatal outcomes, we examined associations between neighborhood stress and social vulnerability, and placental metals concentrations. Pregnant participants (n = 242) in the UPSIDE study (Rochester, NY) completed the City Stress Inventory which has two subscales: neighborhood disorder (e.g., vacant buildings) and violence (personal experiences of violence). Neighborhood disorder was considered as quartiles (Q) and violence was considered binary (any/none). Participant addresses were linked to the CDC's Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and its four sub-themes (socioeconomic status, household composition and disability, minority status and language, housing type and transportation). SVI assigns each census tract a U.S.-wide percentile ranking (0-1) with higher values indicating greater vulnerability). We categorized SVI measures as low, medium [M], and high. At delivery, placenta were collected and lead, arsenic, cadmium, chromium, and manganese were analyzed by ICP-MS. We fitted adjusted linear regression models associating neighborhood stress and SVI measures with each log-transformed metal. Results are reported as percentage difference (%∆) in metal concentrations. Most participants (73%) reported exposure to neighborhood disorder, 24% reported exposure to neighborhood violence, and overall SVI had a median of 0.4 and IQR of 0.5. Compared to the lowest disorder quartile, higher neighborhood disorder was associated with higher cadmium (Q2:%∆=25.5, 95%CI:0.3,57.1). Positive associations were observed for minority status and language vulnerability with cadmium (M:%∆=26.4, 95%CI:2.9,55.1) and housing type and transportation with chromium (M:%∆=27.1, 95%CI:1.3,59.6) compared to the lowest tertile. Some aspects of neighborhood stress and social vulnerability were associated with placental metals concentrations, which may have implications for perinatal health.

title: The active self in autism: multisensory and sensorimotor foundations of bodily self-representation.
abstract: The active self, understood as the embodied sense of self arising from goal-directed action and interaction with the environment, is supported by sensorimotor processes including multisensory integration and proprioception. Atypical self-representation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been proposed to relate to differences in these processes. To clarify this relationship, we conducted a systematic conceptual review of 37 empirical studies published between 2010 and August 2025 examining multisensory and bodily components of the active self in ASD. The literature was synthesized across three themes: (1) multisensory integration, (2) self-bias and self-other differentiation, and (3) motor underpinnings of bodily awareness. Across studies, autistic participants frequently showed differences in multisensory timing and weighting, including reduced or delayed susceptibility to some bodily ownership illusions and greater reliance on proprioceptive or immediate sensory information. Evidence also indicated differences in the flexibility of peri- and interpersonal space, self-other differentiation, agency-related processing, and motor planning and execution. However, findings were not uniform across paradigms, developmental stages, or participant groups, with relatively preserved performance reported under some unimodal or low-noise conditions. Together, these findings support an association between multisensory and sensorimotor processing and several components of bodily self-representation in autism, while substantial methodological and sample heterogeneity limits strong causal or clinical conclusions. Future research should prioritize larger and more representative samples, longitudinal and multimethod designs, standardized experimental paradigms, and objective measures of embodiment to determine whether these mechanisms can ultimately inform individualized assessment and intervention.Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: The effects of mirabegron and anticholinergic treatment on anterior segment and pupillary responses in overactive bladder syndrome.
abstract: To evaluate the effect of tolterodine and mirabegron on anterior chamber parameters and static pupillometry measurements in overactive bladder (OAB) patients and to compare these results with those of healthy controls. This study included 35 patients with OAB who were planned to be treated with tolterodine, 35 patients with OAB who were planned to be treated with mirabegron, and 35 healthy control subjects. All the participants underwent full ophthalmic examination and scanning with Sirius topographer (CSO, Firenze, Italy) before and at 1 and 3 months in both the control and the mirabegron and anticholinergic groups after treatment. In addition, central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber depth, angle, and volume were recorded. The mean intraocular pressure (IOP) increased significantly in the first month of treatment after mirabegron (p = 0.034). Anterior chamber depth increased significantly in the mirabegron group at the third month of treatment compared to pretreatment (p = 0.039). Higher mesopic and photopic pupil diameters were found at 1 and 3 months after tolterodine compared to baseline (p 0.05 for all). Our study demonstrated that both tolterodine and mirabegron affected pupil diameters under different light conditions. They also caused changes in anterior chamber parameters. However, given the modest magnitude of these changes and the dynamic nature of pupil diameter, caution should be exercised in the clinical interpretation of the results.

title: Leveraging Preclinical Models to Understand Human Neurobiology and Behavior.
abstract: Rodent models have become indispensable tools for investigating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying human behavior and disease. Despite the substantial phenotypic differences between rodents and humans, shared evolutionary history, conserved genomic architecture, and analogous neural circuitry allow preclinical findings to meaningfully inform our understanding of human conditions. This chapter reviews the behavioral paradigms most commonly used to evaluate five core domains in rodent models: motor function, stress and anxiety-like behavior, repetitive and restrictive behaviors, social behavior, and learning and memory. For each domain, we describe established assays, discuss the underlying innate behaviors they leverage, and highlight examples in which preclinical data have advanced mechanistic understanding or therapeutic development for human neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. We emphasize that behavioral findings must be interpreted with careful precision, as rodent behaviors are not direct equivalents of humans' intentional, complex behaviors or human emotional states but rather analogous outputs of neural circuits that can be operationally quantified. Throughout this chapter, we highlight critical considerations for rigor and reproducibility, an ongoing issue in the preclinical rodent behavioral space, such as the influence of environment; the appropriate selection of control groups; the importance of litter effects and background strain; and sex as a biological variable. Taken together, this chapter provides both a practical guide to preclinical behavioral neuroscience and a framework for maximizing the translational value of animal model research.

title: The Importance of Translational Research for Neurodevelopmental Disorders and Autism Spectrum Disorders.
abstract: Translational research is the process of transforming fundamental biological discoveries into safe and efficacious interventions for patients. This specialized field is of particular importance for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), a broad class of behaviorally defined conditions including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDDs), and related disorders. NDDs present unique translational challenges including (i) a lack of biological diagnostic markers; (ii) the fact that they are diagnosed exclusively by behavioral criteria; (iii) their involvement of dysfunction in complex brain circuitry; and (iv) that there is no single unifying biological mechanism. This chapter reviews the current landscape of translational neuroscience for NDDs, examining the strengths and limitations of preclinical model systems, including rodent models humanized mice, human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) 3D spheroids and brain organoids. This work emphasizes that research emanating from the varying preclinical experimental systems above should be leveraged and their complementary strengths integrated, coordinated, and considered collaboratively, to strengthen current knowledge, identify the remaining research gaps, and prioritize future research. We also emphasize the importance of rigorous, reproducible methodology and conservative interpretation of behavioral and functional outcomes. Discussion is presented on key translational bridges or connections that are urgently required to advance the field: bridging non-human model systems to humanized models, identifying and validating translational biomarkers, bridging in vitro and in vivo findings, and developing corroborative alternatives to animal models. It is our stance that integrating multiple complementary model systems, limiting erroneous behavioral inferences, relying on evolutionarily conserved circuits, and prioritizing robust and reproducible outcome measures will reduce failures in the translational pipeline and accelerate the development of meaningful therapies for individuals with NDDs.

title: Translational Neuroscience of Autism Spectrum Disorder : Genetics: Contribution Not Correlation.
abstract: Ever since the observation of a robust heriditary component of autism, the scientific community has invested efforts and resources toward the identification of genetic variation associated with this condition. The current chapter provides an overview of of these efforts in a historical context, outlining how increasingly precise methods to query the genome along with unprecedented levels of international collaboration are starting to eludicate the complex genetic architecture of autism.

title: Vilazodone Hydrochloride-Loaded Nanostructured Lipid Carrier In Situ Gel for Intranasal Nose-to-Brain Antidepressant Delivery.
abstract: The Oral delivery of vilazodone hydrochloride (VLZ), a serotonin partial agonist-reuptake inhibitor for major depressive disorder, suffers from extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, food-dependent absorption, and poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, limiting its central therapeutic impact. Here, VLZ-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) were engineered and embedded within a Poloxamer 407/188-chitosan thermosensitive in situ gel to enable direct nose-to-brain delivery. The NLCs were fabricated by combined high-shear and high-pressure homogenisation and optimised through central composite design, yielding a batch with particle size 24.74 ± 2.23 nm, polydispersity index 0.248 ± 0.012, and entrapment efficiency 91.37 ± 4.56%. The lyophilised NLCs were incorporated into an in situ gel with a physiologically appropriate gelation temperature of 34°C and gelation time of 42 s. Fourier Transform Infrared FTIR spectroscopy confirmed complete drug encapsulation, evidenced by disappearance of the diagnostic nitrile (C≡N) absorption band, while DSC and XRPD verified conversion of VLZ to an amorphous state within the lipid matrix. Drug release followed Korsmeyer-Peppas kinetics, sustained over 24 h, and the formulation remained stable under refrigerated storage. In Swiss albino mice, the intranasal NLC-in situ gel (1 mg/kg) produced a profound antidepressant-like effect relative to oral pure drug (10 mg/kg) across open field, tail suspension, and sucrose preference tests, consistent with enhanced nose-to-brain delivery via the olfactory and trigeminal pathways. Hence this nanocarrier-hydrogel strategy offers a promising, non-invasive route to enhanced CNS delivery of antidepressants.

title: The dual role of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis in glial cell survival and neuroinflammation.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis is characterized by a triad of inflammation, demyelination, and neurodegeneration, yet current disease-modifying therapies are limited in their ability to halt progressive neurodegeneration or promote remyelination. The PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway is a master regulator of these divergent cellular processes and therefore represents a biological paradox in multiple sclerosis. In the pathogenic facet of the disease, activation of this axis supports the differentiation and effector functions of pro-inflammatory T- and B-cells and contributes to inflammatory programs in microglia and macrophages. In the regenerative facet, physiological PI3K/AKT/mTOR activity is required for oligodendrocyte precursor-cell survival, differentiation, myelin synthesis, and maintenance of myelin integrity. Astrocytic signaling adds another layer of context-dependence, with pathway activity influencing reactive gliosis and the inflammatory or reparative properties of the lesion environment. Consequently, systemic inhibition of the pathway may suppress neuroinflammation while simultaneously interfering with endogenous repair. This review therefore considers PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis according to these opposing pathogenic and protective functions, highlighting the importance of cell type, disease stage, and treatment timing. Precision strategies capable of selectively suppressing inflammatory signaling while preserving or restoring pro-regenerative activity, potentially through cell-specific molecular targets, may provide a more rational therapeutic approach than generalized pathway inhibition.

title: Insulin-mediated ciliary remodeling in the choroid plexus epithelium.
journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) epithelium plays a crucial role in cerebrospinal fluid production and brain homeostasis. ChP is mainly composed of multiciliated epithelial cells that exhibit a noncanonical ciliary organization whose function is still debated. Insulin signaling is known to be important for central nervous system function, but its role in ChP function and ciliary organization has not been elucidated yet. To investigate how prolonged insulin exposure modulates ChP cells, we treated primary murine choroid plexus epithelial cells (pCPECs) with insulin for up to six days and used a combination of immunohistochemistry, RT-qPCR, RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization, single cell analysis and Western Blot to explore underlying molecular mechanisms. We demonstrated that prolonged insulin treatment significantly increased the percentage of multiciliated clustered pCPECs and their axoneme length. Prolonged insulin treatment selectively induced translocation of IFT20, a key component of the intraflagellar transport system, to the ciliary axoneme by increasing the cytoplasmatic surface area covered by IFT20. To note, the expression of insulin receptors (IRs) in ex vivo ChP epithelial cells started during late embryogenesis and localized predominantly to the apical membrane, but not in the cilium. Our study suggests that insulin signaling may promote ciliary remodeling in choroid plexus epithelial cells, most likely by modulating intraflagellar transport dynamics involving IFT20. These findings reveal a novel role of insulin signaling in ChP cilia organization and function, with potential implications for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) regulation and neurodevelopmental processes.

title: Glutamate tone in preBötzinger complex rhythmogenesis: ambient extracellular glutamate as a candidate excitability bias.
journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology
abstract: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) is essential for inspiratory rhythm generation, yet the biological processes that repeatedly establish the excitability state required for neuronal recruitment remain incompletely understood. This unresolved issue is reflected in computational models of respiratory rhythmogenesis, which rely on a phenomenological baseline excitability parameter, [Formula: see text], without a defined biological substrate. Ambient extracellular glutamate signaling is well established in other brain regions, but its relevance to the respiratory network remains largely untested. Here, we evaluate the hypothesis that ambient extracellular glutamate outside synaptic clefts-termed glutamate tone-represents one biologically plausible candidate for a distributed extracellular network-state variable in the preBötC. We define glutamate tone as a continuously maintained but dynamically regulated extracellular glutamate signal arising from the balance of glutamate release, diffusion, transporter-mediated clearance, and astrocyte-dependent metabolism. We critically review evidence that extracellular glutamate handling can influence respiratory network activity, while emphasizing that direct evidence for a compartment-specific, rhythmogenesis-relevant glutamate tone remains lacking. We then evaluate candidate glutamate-sensing mechanisms, including peri-/extrasynaptic NMDA receptors and metabotropic glutamate receptors, and place them within the established framework of recurrent excitation, intrinsic membrane conductances, and inhibitory circuitry. We propose that glutamate tone, if present, would not generate the inspiratory burst directly, but could bias the excitability landscape from which neuronal recruitment and synchronization emerge. Finally, we outline experimental criteria for distinguishing a causal excitability bias from glutamate signals that merely reflect ongoing network activity.

title: Chemogenetic inhibition of the ventrolateral orbitofrontal cortex disrupts novelty-guided updating of spatial memories and alters hippocampal engram reactivation.
abstract: Adaptive behavior requires revising memories when outcomes deviate from expectations. The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is implicated in representing outcome expectancies, but its role in memory-updating, beyond value-based learning, remains unclear. We tested whether the ventrolateral OFC (VLO) contributes to hippocampal-dependent memory-updating in the Objects in Updated Locations (OUL) task, where novelty-driven exploration provides a behavioral readout consistent with successful updating of spatial information. Using inhibitory DREADDs, in male and female (Swiss Webster and C57BL/6) mice, we suppressed VLO activity during the Updating session, when new object-location information was introduced. Control mice preferentially explored the updated object-location configuration during Updating and discriminated between updated and novel object-location configurations at Test, whereas VLO-inhibited mice did not. VLO inhibition when no updating demand was present did not alter exploration of novel object-location configurations or memory for the original spatial configuration at Test. These results indicate that VLO activity is selectively required when novelty must be interpreted relative to prior experience, implicating this region in evaluating change rather than detecting it. To assess hippocampal ensemble dynamics, we tagged neuronal ensembles, in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) recruited during Updating, followed by quantification of overlap between Updating-tagged cells and ensembles reactivated at Test. We found that VLO inhibition reduced reactivation of Updating-tagged dDG ensembles, paralleling the behavioral impairments observed in the OUL task. These findings support a role for the VLO in hippocampal-dependent memory-updating and extend OFC models beyond reward contexts to include predictive updating of spatial memory representations. Not applicable.

title: Postoperative DWI morphology and neurological worsening after eloquent-area glioma surgery: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: To assess whether the association between postoperative diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and neurological worsening after eloquent-area glioma surgery differs according to lesion morphology. We retrospectively analyzed 139 consecutive patients undergoing resection of eloquent-area supratentorial gliomas (WHO 2-4). Postoperative MRI (< 48 h) classified lesions as sector- or rim-shaped. Neurological status was assessed at discharge and 4-6 months. DWI lesions occurred in 44/139 patients (31.7%; 31 sector-shaped, 13 rim-shaped); 59 (42.4%) worsened at discharge. Overall, DWI positivity alone was not associated with worsening. Sector-shaped DWI lesions were associated with neurological worsening (positive predictive value, PPV of 58.1%) and remained associated after multivariable adjustment (OR 3.83, 95% CI 1.30-11.29), although the confidence interval was wide and the unadjusted association was borderline. Rim-shaped lesions carried a PPV of 38.5%, comparable to the risk in DWI-negative patients (37.9%), and the two morphologies did not differ significantly in direct comparison. Awake craniotomy was also independently associated with worsening, and frontal site with a lower risk. 61% of worsening occurred with negative DWI. A deficit was present at the 4-6 month follow-up in 9 patients (6.5%), all with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and was associated with a ≥ 50% evoked-potential decrease. In this cohort, postoperative DWI positivity was associated with neurological worsening mainly when the lesion was sector-shaped, a finding that requires confirmation in larger series. Rim-shaped lesions showed a risk of worsening similar to that of a negative scan. Most worsening occurs without DWI ischemia, suggesting non-ischemic mechanisms of function-guided surgery. A deficit at follow-up occurred only in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma and was associated with intraoperative neurophysiological changes.

title: The endocannabinoid system and the ageing brain.
abstract: Ageing is accompanied by a progressive decline in homeostatic resilience that increases vulnerability to chronic disease, disability and cognitive impairment. Although unhealthy brain ageing can often be prevented by managing the underlying risk factors, the molecular, cellular and physiological mechanisms that connect risk factors to late-life brain dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This review examines the role of the endocannabinoid system in brain ageing. The endocannabinoid system is a short-range lipid signalling network that helps to maintain neuronal, glial, metabolic and inflammatory homeostasis. Endocannabinoid signalling follows a dynamic lifespan trajectory, with relatively high activity during early adulthood and functional decline during ageing. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of endocannabinoid system activity impairs several processes linked to hallmarks of brain ageing, including neuroinflammatory control, adult neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, cognitive performance, metabolic regulation and epigenetic stability. Conversely, low-dose Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) treatment can ameliorate several ageing-related brain phenotypes in old animals. However, clinical evidence in older humans remains limited, and the therapeutic potential of cannabinoid-based interventions requires further evaluation.

title: Risk of early stroke recurrence and procedural stroke or death in carotid near occlusion patients scheduled for carotid endarterectomy.
abstract: Carotid near occlusion (NO) refers to distal internal carotid artery (ICA) narrowing caused by proximal carotid stenosis (CS). Stroke risk and optimal management of NO remain controversial. Our aim was to determine the prevalence of NO severities, rates of preoperative ischemic cerebrovascular events (iCVEs), 30-day procedural stroke and death, and hyperperfusion syndrome in patients with NO in a prospective CS cohort undergoing carotid endarterectomy (CEA). We reanalyzed posthoc CTAs from 443 symptomatic and asymptomatic CS patients. Subtle NO (s-NO) was defined as a 1.0-mm difference in distal luminal diameter between ipsilateral and contralateral ICA. NO with full collapse (fc-NO) was defined as ≤2.0 mm and/or an ipsilateral-to-contralateral ICA diameter ratio ≤0.42. Conventional stenosis was defined as CS >50% using NASCET criteria. Rates of preoperative iCVEs and 30-day procedural stroke and death were compared between s-NO, fc-NO, and conventional stenosis. NO occurred in 143 (32%) patients: 124 (87%) s-NO and 19 (13%) fc-NO. NO was not significantly associated with increased preoperative iCVEs (7.6% vs 13%, OR 1.82, 95%Cl 0.96-3.47) or procedural stroke or death (5.6% vs 3.3%, OR 1.73, 95%Cl 0.67-4.50) compared with conventional stenosis. After CEA, hyperperfusion syndrome was frequent in NO patients (7.0% vs 2.7%, OR 2.8, 95% CI1.1-7.1). One patient developed fatal hyperperfusion-related intracranial hemorrhage. CTA-detected NO is common, particularly in subtle forms, and important for stenosis assessment and management. Unlike earlier studies, NO was not associated with increased preoperative or procedural stroke or death, but hyperperfusion syndrome after CEA was more frequent.

title: Cabergoline for non-functioning pituitary adenomas: an update on an old clinical controversy.
abstract: Cabergoline has been used off-label for non-functioning pituitary adenomas (NFPAs) for decades, yet its place in management remains controversial. We reappraised the evidence, emphasizing studies from the last 3-5 years and how contemporary natural-history data influence interpretation of radiological outcomes. We conducted a focused PubMed/MEDLINE search from database inception through 27 September 2026, prioritizing comparative studies, recent cohorts, systematic reviews, natural-history studies, translational research, and clinically relevant safety data. Evidence was synthesized narratively. Earlier studies suggested radiological activity, but the only randomized open-label trial showed primarily a radiological signal, with less growth and more shrinkage, rather than established patient-centered clinical benefit. A 2022 meta-analysis estimated at least 20% shrinkage in 19% and an outcome classified as prevention of progression in 50%. Recent data remain inconsistent: a 2022 multicenter comparison found no clear radiological advantage over observation, a 2024 surgery-naive cohort reported shrinkage/stability/growth in 20%/48%/32%, and 2026 real-world and radiotherapy cohorts have not resolved comparative efficacy. Contemporary natural-history studies show that untreated NFPAs may remain stable, regress, or grow unpredictably. No validated molecular or pathological predictor of cabergoline response has emerged. Recent evidence adds context but does not resolve this long-standing controversy or support routine cabergoline therapy for NFPAs. Cabergoline remains off-label and has no established routine role; it should not displace established surveillance, neurosurgical, or radiotherapy strategies. Prospective controlled studies using standardized volumetric imaging and patient-centered outcomes are needed.
